block-race: Two versions of the same payment. Which should the network accept? Watch how the gap between these chains changes the attacker's odds.
Mining is a biased coin flip based on hashrate. Energy is the price of rewriting history, and the honest majority just outspends the liar.

Forget both chains. Only the gap matters, and the coin is rigged seventy to thirty. From three blocks behind, barely 8 in 100 attackers ever reach zero. Each additional block multiplies the remaining catch-up chance by three sevenths.
Satoshi models the attacker's block count as Poisson with mean lambda = z q over p, then sums gambler's-ruin tails.
Tripling the attacker from 10% to 30% inflates risk by ~544x. Adversary size dominates.
What this really buys is finality with no one in charge: the cost of a lie, denominated in energy and time.
gradient-pinball: Why does one training run converge while another flies apart? Follow the ball: the landscape matters, but so does the size of each step.
Measure slope, step against it, repeat. Each step is the locally steepest move.
Step sizes dictate distance. If too large, the system overshoots and diverges.
Momentum acts as a memory of past gradients. Side-to-side bounces cancel, downhill drift compounds.
For a strongly convex quadratic, optimized momentum changes the condition-number scale from kappa to its square root. At kappa one thousand, that is about 32 before constants and log factors.
In high dimensions, most critical points are saddles. Momentum and noise help escape them.
bcml: Can a blockchain make machine learning more accountable? Start with the training record, then ask what that record actually proves.
Record every transaction in the run, and tampering stops being invisible.
Raw data never leaves its owner. Only parameters, transactions and results reach the chain.
But a record proves what happened, not that it was any good. That needs a second mechanism.
Proof of Work agrees by burning electricity on a puzzle worth nothing once solved.
Aim it at the model. Proof of Learning makes training earn consensus; Proof of Deep Learning covers the model.
Proof of Training Quality asks more: not that work happened, but that it helped.
Now the electricity buys a model. And it opens one hard question: how do you prove the run was real?
Then incentives. One contract accepts the data, prices it, and updates the model.
You are paid for the loss you removed. Submit noise and the term turns negative.
Stake a deposit. It comes back if the data holds up, and is forfeited if it does not.
In simulation the honest and the dishonest separate cleanly, and accuracy holds.
Does it work? DeepChain is a Corda prototype trained on MNIST.
Accuracy rises with every party who joins. Throughput falls with every party who joins.
LearningChain shows the same trade: privacy noise buys privacy and costs accuracy.
So the survey ends on the seams: scale, energy, and consensus designed for learning rather than currency.
A review that only sells the idea is worth nothing. One of those seams, proving the training really happened, became my dissertation.
determinism: A simulator is fast on average. Can one late response still break its timing budget?
The numbers are regulation, not goals. A ceiling of 150 milliseconds, input to response.
Every stage spends it. Image generation takes the largest bite.
Not a target. A gate. Miss it and the hours flown do not count.
Helicopters get 100 milliseconds. A hovering rotorcraft is unstable, and the pilot closes the loop faster.
A fixed cadence. At 60 hertz each subsystem gets 16.67 milliseconds.
Mean frame time is 8.6 milliseconds, half the budget. But a deadline is never met on average.
Count the frames instead. Four hours is 864,000 of them.
One bad frame in a thousand, a 99.9% success rate, is 864 stutters a session.
And that assumes failures spread evenly. They cluster, so the real thing is worse.
A simulator is not one computer. It is a rack, all publishing into one frame.
The frame ends with the last host: latency is a maximum.
Reliability composes by multiplication. Nine hosts at three nines give 99.1% clean.
One straggler is enough. A single host at 19 milliseconds makes the frame late for everyone.
So the budget is allocated and enforced per host. A system average constrains nobody.
None of it is real unless it is instrumented while the session runs.
Trust the overrun counter. Step time is sampled, so a spike hides between polls.
One bus overruns, the rest stay clean, and the engineer knows before the qualification test does.
Determinism is not optimised in at the end. It is a budget, enforced every frame, and proven by the instrument you ship with it.
cyberevent: The bank app is down. Can you catch that signal in a flood of ordinary posts?
The difficulty is the ratio. In an open Turkish stream, real events are a handful in a thousand.
That rarity is not an inconvenience to engineer around. It is the centre of the problem.
With no labelled Turkish corpus, the vocabulary comes from a known incident.
Comparing them is what makes a word an attack word.
Each candidate term then faces an A/B test.
Too many keywords and the queue floods with false positives.
Too few and the event is missed, or noticed days late.
So both become acceptance criteria: catch nic.tr on the day, stay under thirty percent false. It met both.
Then the language pushes back. Turkish stacks suffixes, so one stem becomes dozens of surface forms.
To a bag of words those are unrelated tokens. The evidence scatters.
This is the low-resource penalty, and a bigger classifier does not fix it. Stemming does, before the classifier.
Which is the under-reported part: here, preprocessing decides more than the model does.
And count the right thing. Not sentiment, but the entity that can be attacked.
Each entity is judged against its own history, since normal for one alarms another.
On 14 December, nic.tr jumps from two or three mentions to twenty-eight. That is the signal.
Not rounded: 437 documents, 29 detections, 22 real. About 76%.
The seven false positives are published too. Reporting them distinguishes false alarms from missed events.
jira: Forty boats, shared rules, no one steering them all. Could AI agents coordinate the same way?
Local decisions can create order. They can also create congestion.
Now replace the crews with software agents, all looking for work.
One manager must handle every request. Watch the queue grow beyond that manager's capacity.
What if agents read a shared price instead of waiting for assignments?
So stop assigning the work and price it instead. Will this bug be fixed by Friday?
While its liquidity pool is funded, an automated market maker continuously quotes a price, so a trader does not need a matching counterparty.
The curve's slope gives marginal odds. For binary unit payouts, those odds convert to an implied probability: a market quote, not calibrated truth.
If nobody is working on it, the price is cheap. Cheap is the signal to act.
A developer expects to fix the bug and buys YES at ten cents.
They do the work. In this example, passing tests move the price of the shares they hold.
An oracle receives the completion claim and a bond. An unchallenged claim settles.
The price offered a reason to act. But a rising price is not proof of useful work. Who checks the claim?
Now an agent reads the repository and writes its own ticket.
Propose, price, work, settle. The loop can run without a human assigning tasks.
The problem: agents can invent work and get paid for it. A fabricated ticket follows the same path.
Candidate safeguards: bond proposals, prevent self-settlement, and check work artifacts. Even a passing test needs an independent check.
Price suggests the work. Who verifies the result? That is the open problem.
model-heist: Your model has been copied and fine-tuned. Can a faint watermark still link the copy to you? Let's test the idea, and its limits.
A single large perturbation can be conspicuous and can hurt accuracy. A practical mark has to balance detectability against utility.
In this Gaussian teaching model, spread the mark across coordinates. A matched filter makes aligned signal add coherently while independent noise adds in quadrature.
Under the stated Gaussian assumptions this becomes a Z-test. The threshold trades detection power against false alarms.
Inside this model, aggregate evidence grows with breadth while each coordinate stays weak. Correlated noise or a poor reference can erase that advantage.
A norm-bounded scrub can move the score only by its budget. That is a detector bound, not a universal claim that a real watermark cannot be removed.
oracles: An AI says the crop is damaged. Should a contract release the payment?
The contract did not run the model. It only received an answer.
An outside answer cannot verify itself. Something has to cross this trust boundary.
Two approaches: prove the computation, or give others time to challenge the claim.
First, prove that the specified computation was followed. This is the role of zero-knowledge proofs.
The model runs off-chain. A prover generates a proof of its encoded computation.
A verifier checks that proof, without repeating all the model's work. Security depends on the proof system and its implementation.
A valid proof confirms the computation, not the truth of the input or the quality of the model. Those still need checking.
The optimistic approach starts with a claim and time to dispute it, rather than a proof of every computation.
A proposer posts a bond. A challenger also risks a bond, so a dispute has a cost.
Disputed claims go through a resolution process. A successful challenge can cost the proposer its bond.
Without a challenge, the claim settles when time runs out. That requires someone able and willing to catch false claims.
proof-of-learning: Training a model is expensive. Copying its weights is cheap. Can a training record tell them apart, or can that record be forged too?
A model is not born at the finish line. It walks there step by step. The path is the asset, not the endpoint.
The proof records checkpoints, data batches, their hashes, and training settings. Verification checks whether these pieces agree.
The original checker avoids a full re-run. It replays the largest updates, where a naive shortcut is easiest to expose. Later attacks showed that not every spoof leaves that signal.

The design goal is a cost asymmetry: honest proving takes one training run, while forging should cost at least as much. Later attacks showed that plain Proof-of-Learning does not always meet that goal.
SecurePoL adds a second check: a mark woven into the model. A forger must now reproduce both a plausible trajectory and a watermark-consistent ownership signal.

When models are cloned and stolen, what matters is not only what a model knows, but whether it can show how it learned. SecurePoL makes forgery costlier by checking both the trajectory and the watermark.
redundancy-reactor: Three computers agree. Could all three still be wrong? Watch what happens when independent failures become a shared mistake.
In the ideal voter model, the output fails when a majority of channels fail. Independent rare faults make that event scale as a higher power of the channel failure rate.
For rare, independent faults, simply adding voters pushes the failure probability off a cliff.
When faults correlate, the cliff vanishes. Redundancy no longer protects you; they all fail together.
Ariane 5 had two inertial systems running identical software. The backup failed first; the active unit stopped in the next 72 millisecond cycle for the same reason.
You cannot vote out a shared mistake. Design diversity and independent validation can reduce common-mode risk, but they do not guarantee zero correlation.
wm-compare: A copied model, a hidden API, or generated text. Which watermark could you actually check? Start with a pattern in selected weights.
The owner reads the weights and calculates a statistical score.
Crossing the threshold is evidence, not certainty. False positives remain possible.
The catch: this test needs the weights. What if all you have is an API?
If the thief hides the model behind a commercial API, you cannot see the weights to run a Z-test.
Instead, Black-box watermarks train the network to memorize specific 'Trigger' images during training.
You query the API with the Trigger. Normal images work fine, but the Trigger forces a massive, hidden backdoor activation.
Agreement with secret trigger labels supports an ownership claim. Verification needs multiple queries and a stated false-positive threshold.
For Large Language Models, watermarking happens continuously during text generation.
A pseudo-random hash splits the vocabulary into a Green List and a Red List. The distribution is then skewed toward Green.
In this example, the green list covers half the vocabulary. The null expectation is fifty percent green tokens.
This illustrative stream is about seventy-five percent green. Its score depends on token count and assumptions, not a universal percentage guarantee.
Instead of modifying the main task, you branch off the latent layers to train a secret auxiliary classifier.
The auxiliary head provides another verification signal. It shares learned features, so training can still affect the main task.
A thief might discover and prune this auxiliary head to evade the watermark check at inference time.
SecurePoL combines watermark and trajectory checks to raise the cost of tested attacks. Neither check alone makes forgery impossible.
